Each has a different end and is separated into its own clause.

reason: The operative lead of Executive Order 6744-A reads: "do adopt and approve the report, recommendations, and findings of the Administrator and do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved, and shall become effective on the date of this Order", subject to five conditions (clauses 1 to 5). It approves the Retail Tobacco Trade code effective on the date of the order, June 19, 1934. The lead states no period or until-date of its own. The approval was code-dependent: under section 3(b) of the Act the approved provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under section 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under section 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor, so the approval operated only through section 3. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval, so the approval ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not as an end date.

Clause 1 reads: "1. That the provisions of Part I of Article VI and of Schedule I—the Cigar Merchandising Plan—be stayed and shall not become effective until Monday, June 25, 1934.". It stays Part I of Article VI and Schedule I (the Cigar Merchandising Plan) until Monday, June 25, 1934. The stay therefore ends by its own terms on June 25, 1934, the day the stayed provisions are to become effective; the date is recorded as the end under the inclusive reading of the until-date, and the exclusive reading would make the last day of the stay June 24, 1934. Either reading falls before June 14, 1935, so the stay's first end is its own stated date and the later repeal is not its end. The stayed provisions themselves are code provisions that operate from June 25, 1934 as part of the approved code, subject to the later clauses and to the repeal of June 14, 1935 recorded on the lead clause.

Clause 2 reads: "2. That the waiting periods of five and three days contained in Schedule I, Part A, Section 1, and in Schedule I, Part B, Sections 1 and 2, respectively, be stayed and shall not become effective, notwithstanding said cigar merchandising plan becoming effective, until the further order of the Administrator.". It stays the five-day and three-day waiting periods of Schedule I until the further order of the Administrator. The stated end is a contingent event with no date. No held text records such an order, and the held corpus does not include Administrator orders, so the stay is recorded as ending no later than the repeal and not as having ended earlier. The stay concerns a provision of the approved code and has no operation apart from it, so it fell with the approval when section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, effective on approval, June 14, 1935. A held order lifting the stay before that date would become the first end. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

Clause 3 reads: "3. That all provisions for the filing of prices and discounts in said cigar merchandising plan be stayed until arrangements satisfactory to the Administrator, are made for confidential treatment and for simultaneous distribution thereof to all members of the trade and customers willing to pay the cost thereof.". It stays the filing of prices and discounts under the cigar merchandising plan until arrangements satisfactory to the Administrator are made. The stated end is a contingent event with no date, and no held record shows such arrangements made or approved. The stay concerns a provision of the approved code and has no operation apart from it, so it is recorded as ending no later than the repeal, June 14, 1935, under section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 (the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement were repealed, effective on approval). It is not recorded as having ended earlier; a held record of satisfactory arrangements before that date would become the first end. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

Clause 4 begins: "4. That the preamble and Sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6, Part II of Article VI be stayed and that the trade accept in place thereof, the following:" and sets out replacement standards for pricing practices (a prohibition of wilfully destructive price cutting with complaint procedure, no fixed minimum prices when no emergency is declared, and an emergency procedure under which the Administrator may fix a basis for minimum prices for a stated period). It substitutes those standards for the stayed provisions of Part II of Article VI and states no end of its own: its words for a stated period concern future emergency price periods the Administrator may fix, not this clause, and no held record shows any such period fixed. The replacement standards were standards of the approved code and operated only through it, so they ceased to operate when section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, effective June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

Clause 5 reads: "5. That the provisions of Articles III and IV shall be and the same hereby are stayed until, and shall become effective on, Monday, June 25, 1934.". It stays Articles III and IV until, and provides that they become effective on, Monday, June 25, 1934. The stay ends by its own terms on June 25, 1934, recorded under the inclusive reading of the until-date; the exclusive reading would make June 24, 1934 the last day of the stay. Both fall before June 14, 1935, so the stay's first end is its own stated date and the repeal is not its end.
